claims.text: Controlled modification of phosphorus, sulfur, or tin content together with tailored tempering parameters can tune the temper-embrittlement window in conventional low-alloy tempered martensitic steel.
The proposed steel can exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition over a narrow temperature interval.
Typical impurity levels in conventionally forged low-alloy tempered martensitic steel produce pronounced grain-boundary segregation during tempering.
Impurity segregation at grain boundaries embrittles an otherwise ductile martensitic matrix.
At intermediate temperatures, impurities segregate to grain boundaries during tempering.
Grain-boundary impurity segregation causes localized boundary weakening and a loss of ductility.
Controlling impurity level and tempering conditions can shift the onset, width, and recovery of ductility in the embrittlement window.
The resulting ductile–brittle–ductile transition is reversible.
The brittle regime will occupy a narrow and tunable temperature interval.
The steel will remain ductile at temperatures below and above the embrittlement interval.
Increasing impurity content is expected to shift and possibly widen the embrittled regime.
More aggressive tempering is expected to shift and possibly widen the embrittled regime.
Standard low-alloy tempered martensitic steel under conventional tempering conditions displays a characteristic fixed temper-embrittlement window.
Impurity solubility limits may constrain the tunability of the embrittlement regime.
Excessive impurity additions may form deleterious phases and thereby limit useful tuning.
The qualitative effect of impurity segregation on temper embrittlement is well established.
The quantitative ductility shifts and temperature range of the embrittlement window depend on alloy composition and processing details.
